paragraphs: 4D3R reconstructs moving scenes from a single-camera video so they can be rendered from new viewpoints. Its starting challenge is that both the camera and objects may move, while the camera positions are unknown. The framework separates static and moving scene components and estimates camera geometry as part of reconstruction.

The process begins with initial geometry and camera estimates from 3D foundation models, then refines them using motion information. A motion-aware bundle adjustment module combines learned transformer priors with SAM2 segmentation to distinguish moving objects during camera refinement. For rendering, the method represents motion through control points, a neural deformation field, and blended transformations, reducing the computational burden of representing dynamic content.

On real-world dynamic datasets, the authors report improvements of up to 1.8 dB in PSNR over state-of-the-art methods, particularly for scenes with large moving objects. They also report fivefold lower computational requirements than previous dynamic representations. These findings support treating motion estimation, camera refinement, and scene representation as connected parts of the reconstruction problem.
neurips-2025-4d3r-motion-aware-neural-re.tldr: 4D3R jointly handles unknown camera poses and scene motion to improve dynamic reconstruction while reducing computation.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning builds a binary classifier from a small collection of labeled positive examples and a much larger unlabeled collection. This paper examines how existing methods use that incomplete supervision, organizing them into two families. One estimates a supervised learning objective without assigning individual labels to the unlabeled examples; the other assigns provisional labels.

The authors empirically study risk-based approaches including uPU, nnPU, and DistPU. From an aggregate-supervision perspective, they propose a set-aware empirical risk described as risk-consistent. They separately examine pseudo-label estimation methods and commonly used training techniques, asking what these ingredients contribute to learning from positive and unlabeled data.

Those findings motivate a framework that combines the set-aware objective with pseudo-labeling. The contribution is therefore both an analysis of existing design choices and a way to bring the two methodological families together. The authors position the combined framework as a potential practical benchmark for PU learning, rather than claiming that either family alone resolves the task.
neurips-2025-a-closer-look-to-positive-u.tldr: This empirical study organizes positive-unlabeled learning methods and combines set-aware risk estimation with pseudo-labeling.

paragraphs: Mamba offers linear-complexity processing of long sequences, making it a promising alternative to attention-based architectures. This paper uses deliberately constructed synthetic tasks to investigate a more specific question: which kinds of relationships does its architecture find difficult to recognize? The emphasis is on understanding architectural behavior through controlled tasks.

The experiments examine composite functions and matching sequences presented in reverse order. The authors find that Mamba strongly favors compositional solutions and has difficulty with symmetrical relationships, including reversed-sequence matching. They attribute this asymmetry bias to the nonlinear convolution that combines token information before it reaches the state-space module.

That attribution is the central finding: the reported difficulty comes from how information is fused before state-space processing, rather than from the state-space module itself. It identifies a concrete component to reconsider when designing sequence models that must handle symmetry. Because the evidence comes from carefully designed synthetic tasks, the findings describe specific architectural difficulties rather than establishing a universal performance ranking between Mamba and Transformers.
neurips-2025-achilles-heel-of-mamba-esse.tldr: Synthetic tasks identify Mamba’s preceding nonlinear convolution as a source of difficulty with symmetry and reversed-sequence matching.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether competing AI arguments can help evaluators judge controversial factual claims despite their prior beliefs. The researchers compare debate, where two AI advisors argue opposing sides, with consultancy, where an evaluator interacts with one advisor. The claims concern COVID-19 and climate change, topics on which participants may hold strong views.

The first study includes human judges with mainstream or skeptical beliefs. Debate improves both judgment accuracy and the relationship between confidence and correctness, outperforming consultancy by a reported 4–10% across the two topics. The largest gains occur among mainstream judges, while skeptical judges who initially assess claims incorrectly also move toward more accurate judgments.

A second study compares AI judges with and without human-like personas. Persona-based judges reach 78.5% accuracy, compared with 70.1% for humans and 69.8% for default AI judges. Together, the results suggest that debate and evaluator design could contribute to scalable oversight. They support that possibility in the studied contested domains, without establishing that debate eliminates bias.
neurips-2025-ai-debate-aids-assessment-o.tldr: AI debate improved factual judgments and confidence calibration in studies of controversial COVID-19 and climate claims.

paragraphs: Early-exit networks can make predictions at intermediate layers, saving computation when further processing is unnecessary. A common rule stops whenever confidence exceeds a fixed threshold chosen on validation data. The paper addresses two weaknesses of this rule: a model can confidently predict the wrong class, and deployment data can differ from the data used to set the threshold.

The proposed method, UAT, adjusts exit thresholds online through a multi-armed bandit framework. Its adjustments are unsupervised, allowing the exit policy to adapt without labeled deployment examples. A new reward evaluates predictive certainty together with its reliability, balancing prediction quality against computation and penalizing exits that occur unnecessarily late.

The authors provide guarantees on the risk achieved by UAT and evaluate it on vision-language understanding, text generation, and classification. They report speedups of 1.70–2.10 times with a performance reduction below 2% relative to the full model. These results support adapting exit decisions during use instead of relying entirely on a threshold fixed before deployment.
neurips-2025-beyond-greedy-exits-improve.tldr: UAT adapts early-exit thresholds online to balance reliable predictions with computational savings.

paragraphs: Scientific machine learning needs comparisons that reveal which methods work for which problems. This paper argues that weak baselines, selective reporting, and inconsistent evaluations make that difficult. Its proposed Common Task Framework gives competing algorithms shared datasets and task-specific metrics, making their results easier to compare directly.

The framework covers forecasting, reconstructing system states, and generalizing under realistic conditions such as noisy observations and limited data. Its initial benchmarks use the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Lorenz systems. The authors present these evaluations as demonstrations of how common tasks can expose different methods’ strengths, limitations, and suitability for particular objectives.

The next step described is a competition using global sea surface temperature data with a genuinely held-out evaluation set. That competition is an initiative being launched, rather than a completed result in the abstract. The broader contribution is an evaluation structure intended to replace ad hoc comparisons with reproducible assessments on hidden test data, helping researchers judge progress and allocate resources more meaningfully.
neurips-2025-common-task-framework-for-a.tldr: A shared benchmarking framework aims to make scientific machine learning comparisons more rigorous and reproducible.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate unwanted NSFW imagery as well as useful creative content. Concept erasure methods seek to reduce this behavior, but the paper identifies a gap in how their effectiveness has been assessed across different scenarios. Its central contribution is a systematic evaluation effort supported by a toolkit covering the concept-erasure pipeline.

The study connects the mechanisms behind erasure methods with their observed behavior. This makes the assessment concerned with both how a method operates and how it performs in practice. The authors describe the work as the first systematic study of NSFW concept erasure, with coverage intended to inform use across varied real-world situations.

The stated outcome is a set of insights and practical guidance for applying existing erasure methods. The significance lies in giving content-safety research a more comprehensive basis for comparing and understanding these interventions. The abstract presents this as groundwork for better application and further research, rather than as a claim that concept erasure guarantees the absence of unwanted output.
neurips-2025-comprehensive-assessment-an.tldr: This paper introduces a toolkit and systematic assessment of NSFW concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models.

paragraphs: Partial multi-label learning trains models from candidate label sets that contain noise. Prototype-based approaches represent each class with a characteristic pattern and use those patterns to estimate label confidence. However, incorrect candidate labels can bias the prototypes themselves, especially when few positive examples are available.

The paper proposes aligning two sources of class prototypes: those learned through fuzzy clustering and those derived from candidate labels. Two transformation matrices allow these representations to correct one another, with the alignment also updating the soft memberships assigned to labels. This creates a route for revising label confidence without relying exclusively on the noisy candidate assignments.

A learned permutation matrix then helps transform those memberships into a label-reliability matrix alongside the candidate set. The construction prevents values from being assigned outside candidate labels while trying to suppress incorrect candidates. This reliability information guides joint training of label confidence and the classifier. The authors report significant advantages over state-of-the-art partial multi-label methods, supporting the value of correcting prototypes and supervision together.
neurips-2025-confidence-aware-with-proto.tldr: Mutually aligned class prototypes help estimate label reliability and train classifiers from noisy candidate labels.

paragraphs: DeepASA analyzes complex audio scenes in which multiple sounds overlap and their sources may move. It combines source separation, reverberation removal, sound-event detection, audio classification, and direction estimation in one model. The organizing idea is to represent each sound source as an object whose features support several related predictions.

Its pipeline extracts features with a dynamic temporal kernel, aggregates them with a transformer, and separates them into per-object representations. Task-specific decoders then use those representations. Keeping predictions attached to objects resolves the ambiguity of associating separately estimated auditory properties with the correct source, a problem the authors identify in traditional track-based processing.

An early separation mistake can still disrupt later tasks. DeepASA addresses this through temporal coherence matching within an iterative inference process, combining task information and refining object features using estimated auditory parameters. On ASA2, MC-FUSS, and STARSS23, the authors report state-of-the-art results across all evaluated tasks. The findings support a shared object representation for coordinating sound separation and spatial audio understanding.
neurips-2025-deepasa-an-object-oriented-.tldr: DeepASA uses iteratively refined sound-object representations to unify separation, recognition, and spatial audio estimation.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses positive and negative pairs to shape representations without explicit labels. Its usefulness depends on whether these pairs provide meaningful signals. Treating other images in a batch as semantically different can be problematic in settings where examples are similar, motivating closer attention to how training batches are constructed.

This paper shifts attention from choosing individual negative examples to the geometry of the batch as a whole. Its central observation is that diversity across the batch’s embeddings strongly influences both the strength of learning updates and the quality of the representation. Diversity here concerns how examples occupy the learned representation space.

The authors describe two unfavorable extremes. With too little diversity, negatives are nearly identical and gradients can vanish, leading to collapse. With too much diversity, negatives become nearly orthogonal and gradients also shrink, slowing learning. Their conclusion is that effective training occupies a moderate diversity window: enough variation to avoid collapse while retaining strong updates. The argument therefore favors balanced batch geometry rather than simply maximizing diversity.
neurips-2025-diversity-is-all-you-need-f.tldr: The paper argues that contrastive learning benefits from moderate batch diversity because both extremes weaken gradients.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting can reconstruct an opaque object with surfaces that incorrectly behave as transparent. The artifact becomes visible when the camera moves and background or internal patterns appear inconsistent. The paper traces it to training that blends foreground and background Gaussians to match RGB images without explicitly constraining surface opacity.

Noise Guided Splatting addresses this by placing opaque noise Gaussians inside the object during training. Their presence encourages surface Gaussians to become more opaque, with only small changes to the existing rendering process. The intervention targets the ambiguity that allows an apparently good image match to conceal incorrect transparency.

The authors also introduce a transmittance-based metric, an object-focused scan dataset, and noise-augmented versions of existing datasets to assess the artifact. Across multiple datasets, they report substantially reduced false transparency while preserving competitive standard rendering scores such as PSNR. The work shows why evaluating static image similarity alone can miss a reconstruction defect that matters during interactive viewing.
neurips-2025-fix-false-transparency-by-n.tldr: Noise Guided Splatting reduces false transparency by encouraging opaque surfaces during Gaussian-splatting training.

paragraphs: A model’s prediction does not automatically explain what would happen under a hypothetical change. This paper formalizes causal interpretability: when a particular class of models, together with observational data, permits a counterfactual question to be evaluated. That shifts interpretability toward whether specific “what if” questions can actually be answered.

The authors analyze black-box predictors and concept-based predictors, showing that neither is causally interpretable in general. Representing predictions through concepts therefore does not by itself settle counterfactual questions. They develop a framework for designing causally interpretable models and derive a complete graphical criterion for deciding whether an architecture supports a given query.

The analysis exposes a tradeoff between causal interpretability and predictive accuracy. To characterize it, the authors identify a unique maximal feature set that preserves interpretability while providing maximal predictive expressiveness. Experiments corroborate the theory. The contribution is a principled way to connect architecture, available features, and the counterfactual questions a model can support, rather than treating interpretability as an undifferentiated property.
neurips-2025-from-black-box-to-causal-bo.tldr: A graphical criterion identifies which counterfactual questions a model architecture can support and characterizes the associated predictive tradeoff.

paragraphs: HO-Cap provides a capture system and video dataset for reconstructing the shapes of hands and objects and tracking their poses during interaction. The setup combines multiple cameras that record color and depth with a HoloLens headset. It avoids relying on expensive 3D scanners or motion-capture systems for data collection.

The authors also introduce a semiautomatic annotation method for the recorded shapes and poses. They report that this reduces labeling time and cost substantially compared with manual annotation. The capture and annotation components work together to make detailed hand-object interaction data less burdensome to produce.

The dataset contains people manipulating objects with one or two hands, including picking and placing, transferring objects between hands, and using objects according to their functions. These recordings can serve as human demonstrations for embodied AI and robot-manipulation research. The authors state that the capture setup and annotation framework will be made available, extending the contribution beyond the collected videos to a reusable process for creating and tracking 3D interaction data.
neurips-2025-ho-cap-a-capture-system-and.tldr: HO-Cap combines accessible capture hardware and semiautomatic annotation to collect 3D hand-object interaction demonstrations.

paragraphs: InfinityStar uses one discrete autoregressive architecture to generate both images and videos. Its central idea is to model spatial relationships within imagery and temporal relationships across video together. This gives a common framework for text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video, and longer video generation.

For extended videos, the framework continues generation through temporal autoregression: later content is generated in sequence. The unified design connects still-image synthesis and dynamic video synthesis through the same modeling approach. The paper presents this as a route to high-resolution visual generation using a purely discrete representation.

The authors report a VBench score of 83.74, exceeding all autoregressive models in their comparison and diffusion competitors including HunyuanVideo. They also report generating a five-second, 720p video roughly ten times faster than leading diffusion methods without additional optimization. These results support the approach’s combination of quality and speed. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first discrete autoregressive video generator capable of industrial-level 720p output and release its code and models.
neurips-2025-infinitystar-unified-spacet.tldr: InfinityStar unifies discrete autoregressive image and video generation, reporting strong quality and substantially faster video synthesis.

paragraphs: Stackelberg mean field games model a leader interacting with an infinitely large population of homogeneous followers. The leader must improve its own policy while anticipating how the followers respond. This produces a two-level optimization problem, with existing approaches facing restrictive assumptions, inefficient nested training loops, or missing finite-time guarantees.

The proposed AC-SMFG algorithm uses a single actor-critic loop operating on continuously generated Markovian samples. It alternates updates for the leader, a representative follower, and the mean field describing the population. This structure addresses the sampling inefficiency associated with repeatedly solving an inner optimization problem.

The authors prove convergence to a stationary point within finite-time and finite-sample analyses. Their key gradient-alignment assumption allows part of the leader’s gradient to approximate its full policy gradient, relaxing prior leader-follower independence requirements. This is a conditional stationary-point guarantee, not a claim of global optimality. Simulations in established economics environments also show better policy quality and convergence speed than the evaluated multi-agent and mean-field learning baselines.
neurips-2025-learning-in-stackelberg-mea.tldr: AC-SMFG learns leader-follower policies in one loop with finite-sample stationary-point guarantees under a gradient-alignment assumption.

paragraphs: LoRASuite addresses what happens to previously trained LoRA weights when a language model is upgraded. Retraining these task adaptations from scratch can be costly, while weights suited to an older model may no longer work well. The paper proposes transferring existing adaptations through a modular process tailored to different kinds of model updates.

First, LoRASuite computes a transfer matrix from known parameters of the old and new models. It then matches layers using centered kernel alignment and attention heads using cosine similarity. A small subsequent fine-tuning stage supports numerical stability. Together, these steps adapt the earlier weights to the structure and parameters of the upgraded model.

Experiments show consistent gains over small-scale vanilla LoRA training. On MiniCPM and Qwen, the method also exceeds full-scale LoRA retraining on math tasks by average margins of 1.4 and 6.6 points, respectively. The authors report 5.5 GB lower memory consumption and 78.23% less computation time. These findings support reusing prior adaptation work during model upgrades in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-lorasuite-efficient-lora-ad.tldr: LoRASuite transfers existing LoRA adaptations across model upgrades through parameter mapping, structural matching, and small-scale fine-tuning.

paragraphs: MindGYM studies how models can generate training questions that improve transferable reasoning. Its approach guides data synthesis with explicit cognitive objectives, aiming to move beyond rigid question templates and dependence on human-written instruction collections. The framework organizes question creation into a progression from simple reasoning seeds to more demanding combinations.

First, high-level thinking objectives shape the model’s synthesis behavior. Next, it generates single-hop questions across diverse semantic types. Finally, it combines question-answer seeds into challenging multi-hop examples. This structure is intended to broaden the kinds of thinking exercised while increasing the depth of reasoning required.

The authors report that the resulting synthetic data has 16.7% higher average quality and 67.91% lower quality variance than baseline sources. They identify quality and self-contained examples as essential to effective thinking-oriented fine-tuning. MindGYM improves results on six reasoning benchmarks, including gains up to 16% on MathVision with 400 samples, with improvements across model sizes and architectures. These findings support structured self-generated questions as a resource-efficient training approach.
neurips-2025-mindgym-what-matters-in-que.tldr: MindGYM builds cognitively guided questions from simple seeds to multi-hop challenges, improving reasoning with small synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: POLAR reframes reward modeling as distinguishing between policies. Instead of learning only absolute preferences, a reward model represents the relative difference between a training policy and a target policy with desired behavior. That difference supplies a signal for moving the training policy toward the target.

The pretraining objective teaches the model to recognize identical policies and distinguish different ones. The authors use this approach to build reward models ranging from 1.8 billion to 7 billion parameters. The intended advantage is a scalable objective that can capture general ranking relationships across different targets.

Reported results include preference accuracy increases from 54.8% to 81.0% on STEM tasks and from 57.9% to 85.5% on creative writing for POLAR-7B relative to the stated baselines. Reward-guided fine-tuning also raises average policy performance across 20 benchmarks for LLaMa3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-32B. Scaling experiments show a power-law relationship between computation and performance, with correlation coefficients approaching 0.99. These empirical findings suggest that policy discrimination is a promising foundation for more general reward models.
neurips-2025-pre-trained-policy-discrimi.tldr: POLAR pretrains reward models to distinguish policies, improving preference judgments and reward-guided language-model training.

paragraphs: This position paper calls for a prohibition on using generative AI to control, direct, guide, or govern weapons. Its scope includes systems operating locally and remotely. The proposal addresses government agencies and nongovernmental organizations, framing weapon-related use of generative AI as a matter requiring an explicit institutional restriction.

The authors base their position on the unreliability of generative AI and the possibility that its use in these environments could lead to loss of life. Hallucinations are the specific reliability issue identified. The argument connects that issue to the proposed restriction: systems whose hallucinations cannot be successfully modeled and predicted should not have these roles in weapon operation.

The proposed moratorium has a stated endpoint: it should remain until hallucinations can be successfully modeled and predicted. That condition defines the duration the authors advocate; it does not itself establish that satisfying it would make weapon use safe. The paper’s contribution is a policy position about acceptable reliability in potentially lethal settings, rather than an experimental evaluation of a weapon-control system.
neurips-2025-prohibiting-generative-ai-i.tldr: This position paper advocates prohibiting generative AI in weapon control until hallucinations can be successfully modeled and predicted.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation requires identifying relevant regions in images, but expert annotations are scarce and expensive. Although the Segment Anything Model performs well on general segmentation tasks, applying it directly to medical images can yield weaker results. This paper develops a semi-supervised framework built entirely around SAM to address that mismatch.

An efficient SAM variant serves as the student network, and its default prompt embedding is updated during learning. The original SAM acts as a teacher, transferring prior knowledge to the smaller model through hierarchical knowledge distillation. Dynamic weighting adjusts the contributions of the training losses, combining these components into a strategy for learning with limited annotations.

Across several medical datasets, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation approaches. The resulting model uses less than one-tenth of the original SAM’s parameter count, reducing storage and deployment overhead. The findings support using a large foundation model’s knowledge to train a compact medical segmentation model, while adapting the student rather than relying on direct application of the original model.
neurips-2025-segment-anything-model-meet.tldr: A compact SAM student learns from the original SAM to improve semi-supervised medical segmentation with far fewer parameters.

paragraphs: This paper presents two probability bounds for symmetric random matrices whose eigenvalues are bounded. Such bounds describe deviations associated with estimating a mean from random observations. The central feature is adaptation to unknown variance: the inequalities are empirical and available in closed form, whereas the comparison matrix Bernstein inequality requires variance knowledge.

The authors use “sharp” in a precise asymptotic sense. For both new inequalities, the leading deviation term, which scales as one over the square root of the sample count, matches the matrix Bernstein bound exactly, including its constants. This concerns the first-order term as the sample count grows, rather than asserting exact equality of the complete bounds at every sample size.

The first result applies to the sample mean of independent matrices. The second handles a mean estimator with martingale dependence and remains applicable at stopping times. Together, the results cover both independent observations and a specified dependent setting, while retaining tight variance adaptation in the leading asymptotic term.
neurips-2025-sharp-matrix-empirical-bern.tldr: Two empirical matrix concentration bounds adapt to unknown variance while asymptotically matching the leading term of variance-informed Bernstein bounds.

paragraphs: STARC-9 is a colorectal cancer tissue-image dataset designed to address limited morphological diversity, class imbalance, and poor-quality tiles in existing resources. It contains 630,000 image tiles from whole-slide images of 200 patients at Stanford, with 70,000 examples in each of nine clinically relevant tissue classes.

The accompanying DeepCluster++ curation framework combines automated selection with expert verification. An encoder trained on histopathology images extracts tile features, and K-means groups tiles with similar morphology. Equal-frequency binning then samples varied patterns within each tissue class. Gastrointestinal pathologists verify the selected tiles, combining diversity-focused selection with checks on classification accuracy.

The authors benchmark convolutional networks, transformers, and pathology-specific foundation models on tissue classification and segmentation. Models trained with STARC-9 show superior generalizability compared with those trained on the public datasets in the study. The authors also report reduced manual curation effort. Although colorectal cancer is the demonstrated use case, they describe DeepCluster++ as a flexible framework for assembling datasets from other cancer and non-cancer slide repositories.
neurips-2025-starc-9-a-large-scale-datas.tldr: STARC-9 combines balanced tissue classes, diversity-aware sampling, and pathologist verification to improve colorectal tissue-model generalizability.

paragraphs: SLiCEs provide a common framework for sequence models whose state updates use structured, input-dependent matrices. The goal is to retain the expressive capacity of dense matrices while reducing computation. The framework includes existing block-diagonal recurrent models and DeltaNet’s diagonal-plus-low-rank structure, alongside new sparse and Walsh-Hadamard variants.

The theoretical result shows that SLiCEs using block-diagonal, sparse, or Walsh-Hadamard matrices match the maximal expressivity of dense matrices. The authors contrast this with the diagonal transitions used by S4D and Mamba. This matters because computational structure need not sacrifice the expressivity established in their analysis.

Empirically, SLiCEs solve the A5 state-tracking benchmark with one layer and achieve the strongest length generalization among the compared parallel-in-time models on regular-language tasks. On six multivariate time-series classification datasets, they match log neural controlled differential equations while reducing average training-step time twentyfold. The results connect the expressivity analysis to practical sequence tasks, showing both generalization benefits and substantial training efficiency in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2025-structured-linear-cdes-maxi.tldr: SLiCEs use structured state transitions to preserve dense-matrix expressivity while enabling efficient sequence modeling.

paragraphs: Binary code similarity detection asks whether pieces of compiled code are similar despite offering less information and less meaningful syntax than source code. The task matters for applications such as vulnerability and malware detection. This paper investigates how pretrained language models can be adapted to produce useful representations for binary similarity.

The authors first find that pretrained models are mostly capable of recognizing similar binary code even without task-specific training. They then combine several supervised training ingredients: data augmentation, translation-style causal learning, LLM2Vec, and cumulative GTE loss. The combined procedure turns a generic model into a specialized binary-code embedding model.

The reported system substantially exceeds both zero-shot language models and state-of-the-art binary similarity methods. An ablation study examines the training approach, and the authors report robustness across changes in optimization, architecture, and obfuscation. These findings support adapting existing coder models for binary analysis, with the combined training strategy providing a stronger similarity representation than the starting model in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-transforming-generic-coder-.tldr: Combined supervised training turns generic coder language models into effective binary-code similarity embedding models.

paragraphs: Some generative models produce samples that remain on the data’s support even when their learned dynamics contain errors. The distribution of samples may change along that support without moving away from it. This paper studies that distinction using dynamical systems analysis of stochastic and deterministic generation processes.

A perturbation analysis shows that, for a broad class of models, infinitesimal learning errors alter predicted density only on the data manifold. The authors connect this robustness to the alignment of the most sensitive perturbation directions, called top Lyapunov vectors, with tangent spaces along the manifold boundary. They prove a sufficient condition on the generating dynamics for this alignment.

The alignment condition is efficient to compute and, in robust models in practice, yields accurate estimates of the manifold’s tangent bundle. The analysis covers sample paths and probability flows, including conditional flow-matching and score-based models. Its infinitesimal and linear-perturbation setting is central to interpreting the result: it explains support robustness under the analyzed errors without guaranteeing robustness to arbitrary modeling mistakes.
neurips-2025-when-and-how-can-inexact-ge.tldr: A dynamical analysis explains how infinitesimal modeling errors can change sample density without pushing samples off the data support.
